1b:["$","div",null,{"className":"lg:col-span-8","children":[["$","header",null,{"className":"mb-12","children":[["$","h1",null,{"className":"font-serif font-light text-5xl md:text-6xl text-navy mb-4 leading-tight","children":"Ira Glass"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"w-24 h-[2px] bg-gold"}]]}],["$","section",null,{"className":"prose prose-navy max-w-none","children":[["$","div",null,{"className":"relative mb-12","children":[["$","$L1a",null,{"ref":"$undefined","iconNode":[["path",{"d":"M16 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"rib7q0"}],["path",{"d":"M5 3a2 2 0 0 0-2 2v6a2 2 0 0 0 2 2 1 1 0 0 1 1 1v1a2 2 0 0 1-2 2 1 1 0 0 0-1 1v2a1 1 0 0 0 1 1 6 6 0 0 0 6-6V5a2 2 0 0 0-2-2z","key":"1ymkrd"}]],"className":"lucide-quote absolute -left-8 -top-8 h-16 w-16 text-gold/10 pointer-events-none"}],["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Biography"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed prose prose-navy max-w-none  prose-headings:font-serif prose-headings:font-bold prose-headings:text-navy  prose-h3:text-3xl prose-h3:mt-10 prose-h3:mb-4 prose-a:text-gold hover:prose-a:text-navy prose-a:transition-colors prose-img:rounded-md prose-img:shadow-md prose-img:mx-auto prose-img:border prose-img:border-gold/20 prose-blockquote:border-l-4 prose-blockquote:border-gold prose-blockquote:pl-8  prose-blockquote:italic prose-blockquote:text-navy/80 prose-blockquote:font-serif prose-blockquote:text-2xl prose-blockquote:ml-8 prose-blockquote:my-10 [&_blockquote_p::before]:hidden [&_blockquote_p::after]:hidden","children":[["$","h3","h3-0",{"children":"Introduction"}],"\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":["Ira Glass (1924 – 2009) stands as one of the most revered figures in Bahamian maritime history, an iconic Exuma sloop skipper, master boatwright, and foundational patriarch of the National Family Island Regatta [1]. Born into the rugged maritime communities of the Exuma archipelago, Glass spent the better part of a century embodying the ingenuity, resilience, and seafaring artistry of the Bahamian Out Islands [2]. In the crystalline turquoise amphitheater of Elizabeth Harbour off George Town, Exuma, he earned legendary renown across the archipelago for his razor-sharp tactical instincts at the wooden tiller, his peerless command of pry-board human ballast, and his supernatural ability to read the subtle wind shifts and treacherous tidal currents sweeping between Great Exuma and Stocking Island [3]. Alongside contemporary Out Island giants such as ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"captain-rolly-gray","href":"/profiles/captain-rolly-gray","children":"Captain Rolly Gray"}],", Glass helped elevate traditional Bahamian workboat sailing from an endangered subsistence trade into the undisputed premier sporting and cultural showcase of the nation [4]. Beyond the thunder of the racecourse, Glass was an acclaimed master shipwright who crafted, repaired, and tuned wooden sloops using native hardwoods hewn strictly \"by eye,\" preserving centuries of indigenous Bahamian naval architecture [5]. Through his generous, decades-long mentorship of generations of young Exumian sailors, riggers, and shipwrights, Ira Glass ensured that the sacred bond between Bahamian islanders and the sea remained vibrant, indomitable, and permanently etched into the cultural identity of the Commonwealth of the Bahamas [6]."]}],"\n",["$","p","p-1",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/e4/Exuma_and_Cays_in_Bahamas.svg","alt":"A district locator map highlighting Exuma within the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, the archipelago where Ira Glass forged his sailing and boatwright legacy."}]}],"\n","$L1d","\n","$L1e","\n","$L1f","\n","$L20","\n","$L21","\n","$L22","\n","$L23","\n","$L24","\n","$L25","\n","$L26","\n","$L27","\n","$L28","\n","$L29","\n","$L2a","\n","$L2b","\n","$L2c","\n","$L2d","\n","$L2e","\n","$L2f","\n","$L30","\n","$L31","\n","$L32","\n","$L33","\n","$L34","\n","$L35","\n","$L36","\n","$L37","\n","$L38","\n","$L39"]}]]}],"$L3a","$L3b",false]}],"$L3c"]}]

1d:["$","h3","h3-1",{"children":"Early Life and Maritime Heritage in Exuma (1924–1940s)"}]
1e:["$","p","p-2",{"children":["Ira Glass was born in Exuma in 1924, an era when daily life across the Out Islands (later officially designated the Family Islands) was defined by geographic isolation, maritime subsistence, and profound communal solidarity [1]. Stretching across a sweeping crescent of more than 365 cays, islets, and reefs, Exuma possessed virtually no modern infrastructure, paved roads, electricity, or motorized transport in the early twentieth century [7]. Connection between the settlements and the colonial metropolis of Nassau was governed entirely by the seasonal trade winds, the tides, and the seaworthiness of handcrafted wooden hulls [8]. The historical consciousness of Exuma—forged by the defiant rebellion of ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"pompey","href":"/profiles/pompey","children":"Pompey"}]," against chattel enslavement and sustained by generational settlements such as George Town, Rolle Town, Steventon, and the northern cays—nurtured an extraordinary culture of self-reliance and nautical craftsmanship [8]."]}]
1f:["$","p","p-3",{"children":["Raised along the shores of Great Exuma, young Ira developed an instinctive connection to the Atlantic Ocean and the shallow Bahama Banks almost before he could walk [2]. In an Out Island community where every family depended upon fishing, conching, sponging, and coastal freighting to survive, the sea was both classroom and livelihood [7]. Glass spent his boyhood watching local elders fell indigenous trees in the coppice, adze curved timbers on the shoreline, and hand-sew heavy canvas with palm needles and sailmaker's twine [5]. Long before he was entrusted with a commercial vessel, he experimented with hydrodynamics by carving miniature toy hulls out of ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"camalami"}]," wood and dried coconut husks, outfitting them with flour-sack sails and lead fishing sinkers to race them across the bonefish shallows [3]. By his mid-teens, Glass joined the working fleet as an active crewman, navigating cargo sloops and fishing smacks across the treacherous coral heads of the Great Bahama Bank and the abyssal drops of the Exuma Sound [6]. These formative voyages endowed him with an encyclopedic, sensory literacy of Bahamian waters—teaching him to read water depth by shifting shades of emerald, aquamarine, and deep indigo long before the introduction of electronic sounders or nautical charts [7]."]}]
20:["$","p","p-4",{"children":["$","img","img-0",{"src":"https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/eb/Northern_Exuma_Islands_%28Bahamas%29_1.jpg","alt":"The turquoise waters and cays of Exuma, the traditional waters navigated and raced by Bahamian sloop captains."}]}]
21:["$","h3","h3-2",{"children":"Master Boatwright: The Art and Geometry of the Bahamian Sloop"}]
22:["$","p","p-5",{"children":"While Ira Glass earned legendary acclaim with a wooden tiller in his hand, his deepest genius was forged in the boatyard as a master shipwright [5]. The traditional Bahamian working sloop represents a singular triumph of vernacular marine engineering, developed over two centuries to meet the unforgiving conditions of the archipelago [9]. Across the shallow banks and reef passes, European-style deep-keel vessels were useless; Bahamian builders required a vessel with a broad beam, a shallow wooden draft, massive cargo carrying capacity, and exceptional speed under canvas to outrun sudden tropical squalls [9]."}]
3d:T408,Like the revered boatbuilders of Long Island, Andros, and Abaco, Glass constructed sloops strictly "by eye," without blueprints, formal drafting plans, or computerized calculations [5]. Instead, he worked from half-hull carved wooden models and intuitive geometric memory passed down through oral tradition [10]. Glass regularly ventured into the dense coppice forests of Great Exuma in search of naturally grown curves and crooks in the limbs of wild tamarind, dogwood, madeira, and horseflesh trees [10]. These hard, resinous native woods provided natural structural "knees" and ribs that retained their grain and tensile strength far better than saw-milled lumber [5]. Working with adzes, broadaxes, and hand drawknives, he hewed each rib to fit the curvature of the keel, fastening them with copper rivets and galvanized drift bolts [9]. For the topside planking, he shaped long strakes of native yellow pine, carefully steaming and bending them into place before caulking the seams with rolled oakum and boiling pine pitch [5].23:["$","p","p-6",{"children":"$3d"}]
24:["$","blockquote","blockquote-0",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"A Bahamian sloop is alive from the moment her keel is laid. You do not just build a boat out of wood; you listen to the timber, you shape her lines to dance with the Exuma tide, and you balance her until she answers every breath of the wind.\"\n— Ira Glass on traditional Out Island boatbuilding"}],"\n"]}]
25:["$","p","p-7",{"children":"Glass's technical mastery extended into the complex craft of sailmaking and spar fabrication [3]. Traditional Bahamian sloops are radically overpowered vessels, featuring an immense wooden mast stepped far forward and a long wooden boom that overhangs the transom by ten to fifteen feet [9]. Glass possessed a rare gift for cutting and seaming heavy cotton duck canvas to achieve the optimal aerodynamic draft, creating sails with just enough belly to drive a heavy wooden hull through choppy seas while maintaining the flat leech necessary to point close to the wind [3]. He spent countless hours fine-tuning mast rake, shroud tension, and the placement of internal ballast—carefully shifting lead ingots and iron pig ballast along the bilge—to ensure that the vessel maintained a light, responsive helm under full canvas [10]."}]
26:["$","h3","h3-3",{"children":"The Regatta Arena: Elizabeth Harbour and Pry-Board Mastery"}]
27:["$","p","p-8",{"children":["In April 1954, a pivotal cultural renaissance swept the Bahamian Out Islands when American yachtsman and Exuma resident ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"linton-rigg","href":"/profiles/linton-rigg","children":"Linton Rigg"}],", along with prominent Bahamian yachtsmen including Bobby Symonette (son of Premier ",["$","$L1c","a-1",{"slug":"roland-symonette","href":"/profiles/roland-symonette","children":"Sir Roland Symonette"}],"), established the inaugural Out Island Regatta in Elizabeth Harbour at George Town, Exuma [11]. The event was organized out of a pressing cultural necessity: the post-World War II emergence of diesel marine engines and motorized mailboats threatened to render the traditional wooden working sloops entirely obsolete [11]. The regatta created a competitive arena where working watermen could showcase their seamanship and keep the art of wooden sailcraft alive [9]."]}]
28:["$","p","p-9",{"children":"For Ira Glass, the establishment of the regatta in his home waters of George Town transformed his vocation into an arena of national sporting glory [3]. Elizabeth Harbour, sheltered on the east by Stocking Island and opening into the deep sound through narrow ocean cuts, provided an unrivaled natural amphitheater for sloop racing [12]. However, racing an overpowered Bahamian sloop in Elizabeth Harbour demanded an extreme level of athletic choreography, centered upon the unique mechanism of the \"pry board\" [4]."}]
29:["$","p","p-10",{"children":["Because traditional Bahamian sloops lack the heavy external lead keels that keep modern yachts upright, they rely entirely upon dynamic human ballast to balance the colossal pressure of their towering sails [9]. Pry boards—locally known simply as ",["$","em","em-0",{"children":"prys"}],"—are heavy, resilient wooden planks, measuring fourteen to sixteen feet in length, that slide across the deck under heavy iron straps or wooden cleats [10]. When a sloop sails close-hauled on the wind, a crew of eight to twelve athletic sailors scrambles out onto these planks, perching suspended several feet above the rushing sea on the windward side [4]."]}]
2a:["$","p","p-11",{"children":"Under Captain Ira Glass's command, pry-board maneuvers were executed with clockwork precision [3]. Every tack across Elizabeth Harbour was a high-stakes gamble: as Glass pushed the wooden tiller to bring the bow through the wind, the crew had to scramble inward, haul the cumbersome pry planks across the rolling deck, and throw themselves out over the opposite rail before the immense mainsail caught the wind on the new tack [4]. If the crew moved too slowly, the massive spread of canvas would immediately capsize the vessel; if they shifted weight too early, the boat would lose headway and stall in stays [10]. Glass commanded his crews with steady, calm authority, his voice cutting through the whistling gale and foaming spray, balancing his boat on a knife's edge to gain critical boat-lengths against his rivals [3]."}]
2b:["$","h3","h3-4",{"children":"Tactical Prowess and Sloop Trimming in the National Family Island Regatta"}]
2c:["$","p","p-12",{"children":"Throughout the 1950s, 1960s, and 1970s, as the Out Island Regatta expanded into the prestigious National Family Island Regatta, Ira Glass cemented his standing as one of the most brilliant skippers in the history of the competition [1]. Competing across Class A (the twenty-eight-foot heavyweight giants), Class B, and Class C divisions, Glass faced fierce competition from master skippers representing every major maritime island in the colony—including Long Island, Andros, Ragged Island, and Cat Island [11]."}]
2d:["$","p","p-13",{"children":"Glass became celebrated among regatta spectators and competitors alike as an intellectual tactician who could consistently out-think and out-sail faster vessels [2]. He possessed an uncanny understanding of the micro-meteorology of Elizabeth Harbour, knowing precisely where the breeze bent around the contours of Stocking Island, where the wind died in the lee of the high hills, and how the strong tidal current through Conch Cay Cut altered the apparent wind angle [12]. While other captains relied primarily on sheer muscle and sail area, Glass was a master of the starting line, often timing his run to perfection to cross on starboard tack with clear air [3]."}]
2e:["$","blockquote","blockquote-1",{"children":["\n",["$","p","p-0",{"children":"\"In George Town harbour, you can have the fastest boat afloat, but if you do not know where the wind bends off the cays, or how the current pulls through the cuts, you will be left watching Ira Glass’s transom fade away into the spray.\"\n— Family Island Regatta Oral Tradition"}],"\n"]}]
2f:["$","p","p-14",{"children":["His tactical duels against fellow Exuma legend ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"captain-rolly-gray","href":"/profiles/captain-rolly-gray","children":"Captain Rolly Gray"}]," and Long Island's elite skippers drew thousands of spectators to the George Town foreshore and anchored cruising yachts [4]. Glass's hallmark was his daring use of shoal water; understanding the shallow displacement of his sloops, he would frequently cut inside his competitors over shallow sandbars, shaving minutes off the windward leg while his rivals were forced to sail broader, safer courses in deeper water [12]. Moreover, Glass was renowned for his sportsmanship; he regularly lent tools, spare spars, and hand-sewn canvas to visiting crews whose boats had been damaged during the punishing ocean crossing to George Town, ensuring that every island was able to compete on race day [6]."]}]
30:["$","h3","h3-5",{"children":"Mentorship and Passing the Tiller to New Generations"}]
31:["$","p","p-15",{"children":["Following Bahamian independence in 1973 under Prime Minister ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"lynden-pindling","href":"/profiles/lynden-pindling","children":"Sir Lynden Pindling"}],", the Bahamian government and cultural institutions recognized traditional sloop sailing as the foundational sport of national identity [13]. However, as the Bahamian economy rapidly modernized around commercial tourism, financial services, and motorized shipping, the Out Islands faced the danger of losing their traditional maritime trades [7]. Recognizing this threat, Ira Glass dedicated the later decades of his life to educating, training, and mentoring younger generations of Bahamians in Exuma [2]."]}]
32:["$","p","p-16",{"children":"At his waterfront yard in Exuma, Glass operated an informal, open-air nautical academy [5]. He welcomed young boys and apprentices from across the island, teaching them how to read the grain of native timbers, how to handle adzes and drawknives safely, and how to splice wire rope and Manila hemp rigging [6]. In an era when modern fiberglass boat construction was sweeping the world, Glass adamantly maintained that the traditional Bahamian wooden sloop possessed an organic spirit that could never be replicated by synthetic molds [5]. He taught his students that preserving these boats was an act of cultural sovereignty, honoring the ancestral watermen who had built communities across the archipelago with nothing more than native wood and their own hands [8]."}]
33:["$","p","p-17",{"children":"On the water, Glass trained countless young Exumians in the rigorous art of regatta sailing [3]. He instituted strict training regimens for pry-crews, instilling physical endurance, mental composure under pressure, and profound respect for the sea [2]. Many of the prominent Bahamian captains and pry-masters who rose to prominence in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries—competing in the Long Island Regatta, the All-Exuma Regatta, the Cat Island Regatta, and the National Family Island Regatta—traced their nautical education directly back to Ira Glass's deck and workshop [4]. His dedicated mentorship played a decisive role in cementing Exuma's reputation as the undisputed regatta capital of The Bahamas [12]."}]
34:["$","h3","h3-6",{"children":"Honors, Later Years, and Enduring Legacy (1924–2009)"}]
35:["$","p","p-18",{"children":["In his final years, Ira Glass was universally venerated as an elder statesman and maritime patriarch of Exuma [1]. Although he eventually stepped back from the strenuous physical demands of helming Class A sloops in heavy weather, his presence in George Town each April during regatta week remained an indispensable institution [12]. National leaders, regatta commodores, visiting international sailors, and fellow champions—including Olympic gold medalist ",["$","$L1c","a-0",{"slug":"durward-knowles","href":"/profiles/durward-knowles","children":"Sir Durward Knowles"}],"—regularly sought out Glass to glean his insights on sail trim, weather forecasting, and naval craftsmanship [14]."]}]
36:["$","p","p-19",{"children":"Throughout his long life, Glass was honored with numerous community and national tributes celebrating his lifetime of service to Bahamian sports, culture, and craftsmanship [1]. The National Family Island Regatta Committee and local civic organizations repeatedly recognized his historic contributions to the sport, honoring him as a master builder whose craftsmanship had shaped the very fleet that defined Bahamian heritage [12]."}]
37:["$","p","p-20",{"children":"Ira Glass passed away in Exuma in 2009 at the age of eighty-five, marking the end of a golden era in Bahamian wooden boatbuilding [1]. His passing was mourned by regatta communities, sailors, and historians across the entire archipelago [2]. In Elizabeth Harbour, his indelible legacy is rekindled with every blast of the starting gun and every tack of a hand-hewn sloop against the trade winds [3]. As Bahamian sloop sailing continues to thrive as the official national sport of the Commonwealth of the Bahamas, Ira Glass remains immortalized as a master craftsman, a legendary skipper, and an enduring guardian of the nation's maritime soul [5]."}]

3a:["$","$L3e",null,{"title":"Learn about the legacy of Ira Glass","url":"https://caribbeanlegacyarchive.com/profiles/ira-glass-exu"}]
3f:T6e2,Ira Glass made monumental contributions to Bahamian maritime heritage, cultural preservation, and national sports as a master shipwright, premier sloop captain, and foundational icon of the National Family Island Regatta in George Town, Exuma. Across a seafaring career spanning more than six decades, Glass played a decisive role in preserving traditional Bahamian wooden boatbuilding during an era when motorized freighters threatened to extinguish indigenous sailcraft. Constructing vessels strictly "by eye" without blueprints, he mastered the use of native Bahamian hardwoods—such as madeira, dogwood, and wild tamarind—to create sloops celebrated for their hydrodynamic balance, structural durability, and speed under canvas. His technical innovations in hull trimming, mast raking, sail shaping, and internal bilge ballast established the architectural and performance benchmarks that continue to define modern Bahamian Class A, B, and C sloop design.

On the racecourse, Glass was a legendary competitor and tactical pioneer whose peerless mastery of dynamic pry-board human ballast, local wind shears, and tidal currents in Elizabeth Harbour captivated generations of spectators and elevated regatta sailing into the premier showcase of Out Island identity. Beyond his racing triumphs, Glass served as a revered community patriarch who dedicated his later life to mentoring successive generations of Bahamian shipwrights, sailmakers, and skippers. By transmitting ancestral woodworking techniques and tactical seamanship to younger islanders, he safeguarded Exuma's status as the regatta capital of The Bahamas and ensured the survival of traditional sloop sailing, which was ultimately recognized as the official national sport of the Commonwealth.3b:["$","div",null,{"className":"mb-12 pt-12 border-t border-gold/10","children":[["$","h2",null,{"className":"font-serif font-bold text-3xl text-navy mb-6","children":"Major Contributions"}],["$","div",null,{"className":"text-navy/80 text-xl leading-relaxed bg-white p-8 border-l-4 border-tropical-green shadow-sm","children":"$3f"}]]}]
